h: Co-President Adjourns Meeting Early, Nobody Leaves, She Is Forced To Leave Her Own Meeting
b: The agenda concluded at 8:56 PM. Sources confirm she said the words 'that's everything, go home,' collected her laptop, and walked out. Nobody followed her.

Twenty-two members remained in JFF for another forty minutes, arguing about a chart on a deck that is not due until Thursday. At no point did anyone acknowledge that the meeting had officially ended. One member reported eating dinner in the room.
At press time, she had returned for her water bottle, found the room still full, said nothing, and left again.

h: Co-Presidents Have Not Publicly Disagreed Once All Semester, Club Growing Uneasy
b: Members have documented four separate occasions on which both co-presidents began the same sentence, at the same time, at the same volume. A freshman who asked which one he should email was told 'either,' by both of them, simultaneously.

One sophomore attempted to start a rumor that they had argued over a room booking. The rumor died within an hour because, in her words, nobody could picture it. A second member described the dynamic as 'genuinely lovely and also I think about it a lot.'
At press time, an anonymous source had proposed asking them a divisive question in public purely to see what happens, and had been talked out of it by three people who said they were not ready.

h: Client Emails VP Of Engagements At 9 AM Saturday, He Replies In Four Minutes, Neither Acknowledges This
b: The client sent first. This is the detail members keep returning to. A nonprofit director with a family and a functioning life opened her laptop on a Saturday morning to ask a scoping question, and received a four-paragraph answer before her coffee was cold.

The thread ran eleven messages. Nobody typed 'sorry to bother you on a weekend.' Nobody typed 'no worries, happy to help.' Analysts have described the exchange as two people who have completely lost the ability to be normal about a retention strategy.
At press time, the client had sent a follow-up on Sunday, and the Post has been asked not to say how fast he answered.

h: Man Attends Fifteen Minute Coffee Chat, Leaves Ninety Minutes Later Having Changed His Minor
b: He had one question about the interview process. Witnesses at the adjacent table report that by minute forty they were discussing his father, and by minute seventy she was drawing three boxes and an arrow on a napkin.
He did not get his question answered. He has not noticed. Two days later he filed the paperwork to switch, citing the napkin, which he was carrying, which he has since had laminated.
At press time he had scheduled a second coffee chat, telling friends he wanted to 'run one more thing by her,' and had cleared his afternoon.

h: VP Of Social Impact Asks What The Client Actually Needs, Six Weeks Of Work Reduced To A Single Supporting Slide
b: The question came forty minutes into a working session on a market entry strategy the team had been refining since September. Someone had printed the deck. There were tabs in it.

The organization did not need a market entry strategy. The organization needed help keeping the volunteers it already had, a fact available in the second paragraph of an email from week one. The framework now appears on slide thirty-one, where members agree it is doing excellent work.
At press time, the printed copies remained in a drawer in JFF, because nobody on the team has been able to bring themselves to recycle them.

h: VP Of Marketing Changes One Font, Deck Immediately Looks Like It Cost Money
b: Not one figure, recommendation, or slide title was edited. A team member, convinced something else must have changed, opened both versions side by side and compared them slide by slide for eleven minutes before giving up.

The same forty-one slides now read, in the words of a project manager, 'like a document you would hand to a board instead of a document five people made at midnight.' They were, in fact, made at midnight by five people. That has not changed either.
At press time, nobody involved could name the font, all of them were using it, and one member had quietly applied it to a paper for a class in the business school.

h: VP Of Finance Locates Forty Dollars, Attendance At General Meetings Rises Thirty Percent
b: The money was found during a routine review, sitting in a line item that multiple members described as 'the one nobody was in charge of.' It was forty dollars. It had been there since spring.
No programming changed. No emails were sent. Attendance rose anyway, a correlation one member declined to comment on while holding two granola bars and a third in his jacket pocket.
At press time she had projected the fund through December, the room had erupted, and someone in the back had shouted a number at her that she is now, reportedly, considering.

h: VP Of Events Books Room, Room Number On Invite Matches Actual Room, Attendees Visibly Shaken
b: The reservation was real. The building was the correct building. The room contained more chairs than people, and the door was unlocked at the time printed on the invitation, a detail several members initially assumed was aspirational.

There was no group text. There was no wandering. Nobody stood in a hallway holding a laptop. One attendee, arriving to find the event already underway in the advertised location, reported a brief moment of suspicion that he was in the wrong place.
At press time, the projector had also worked, and the Post has been unable to establish whether this was arranged in advance or simply happened.

h: First-Year Mumbles Something Into His Hoodie, PM Stops Entire Room And Makes Him Say It Again
b: The comment was made at low volume and was not intended to be heard. Sources report she raised a hand, stopped a conversation that eight people were already inside of, and asked him to repeat it.
He repeated it. There was a pause. It is now the recommendation, and it is on slide nine with his name in the speaker notes, which he has asked twice to have removed and which remains there.
At press time he had spoken unprompted in three consecutive meetings, a development his roommate described as 'honestly kind of a lot.'

h: PM Reads Entire Appendix, Discovers Slide Nobody On The Team Will Admit To Making
b: The appendix ran nineteen slides, assembled over four weeks by five people, none of whom had read it end to end. She opened it on a Tuesday. She did not resurface until Wednesday.

Among the findings were two contradictions, one chart of unknown origin, and slide fifty-two, which no member of the team recognizes, claims, or can explain. Version history shows it was created at 3:14 AM by an account that everyone insists was not them.
At press time, slide fifty-two had been promoted to the main body of the deck, where it is the strongest slide in the presentation.

h: PM Opens Google Doc, Finds Eleven Anonymous Animals Inside, Greets Each By Name
b: The document had been shared nineteen minutes earlier. By the time he opened it, eleven anonymous animals were moving through the outline, three of them editing the same sentence at once.

He did not ask anyone to identify themselves. Sources report he simply began addressing them individually in the comments, correctly, on the basis of cursor behavior alone. Multiple members confirmed they were 'genuinely a little unsettled' and also 'weirdly touched.'
At press time the outline was finished, and nobody had worked up the courage to ask how he knew which one was the Anonymous Capybara.

h: PM Online At 1 AM Sunday Sending Four Messages, None Of Them About The Deck
b: Activity logs show no edits and no comments. The only entries are four check-ins sent between 12:40 and 1:15 AM, each addressed to a different member, each some version of the question 'are you still up.'

Three of the four were still up. One of them replied 'no,' from his laptop, while editing slide twenty-two, and was told to go to bed. He went to bed. The fourth had been asleep for hours and woke to a message he described as the nicest thing that happened to him all week.
At press time the deck was finished on time anyway, which members note is somehow always how this goes, and which nobody has been able to account for.

h: Faculty Advisor Asks One Eight-Word Question, Six Students Rethink Their Majors, He Was Being Nice
b: It was not a challenge. It was not a correction. Witnesses are unanimous that the tone was warm, curious, and completely devastating, and that he appeared to have no idea what he had done.

The room went quiet for a period estimated at between four and nine seconds. One student later said she had spent two years constructing an answer to a question that had never once been asked out loud in front of her.
At press time the workstream had been rebuilt from scratch, was substantially better, and no member of the team had been able to bring themselves to tell him he caused it.
